publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: It is believed they currently occupy just 7 percent of their historic range. ... Of the nine tiger subspecies that once existed, only six remain (Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers have become extinct in the last 40 years) and the South China tiger is thought to be nearly extinct in the wild.
unsupported: "Around 5,500 tigers remain in the wild", "across thirteen countries" and "A century ago the estimate was near 100,000" (the page gives an older estimate of 1,500 to 3,200 wild tigers); "93 to 95 percent" (the page says they occupy 7 percent of the historic range, so about 93 percent lost)
correctedFact: Tigers are believed to occupy just 7 percent of their historic range, which once stretched across much of southern and eastern Asia to the Caspian Sea. Three of the nine recognized subspecies, the Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers, are already extinct, and the South China tiger is close behind in the wild.
note: The headline number is the card's core and could not be checked: the Smithsonian page carries an outdated 1,500 to 3,200 estimate, and WWF's story on the 2023 Global Tiger Forum estimate of 5,574 returned 403 to every fetch. Range loss and the three extinct subspecies are supported.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Like a human fingerprint, no two tigers have the exact same markings. Because of this, researchers can use stripe patterns to identify different individuals when studying tigers in the wild. ... SCBI scientists are collecting and analyzing a wide range of field data on tigers, prey and mangrove habitat, including through camera-trap studies to estimate tiger populations.
unsupported: "The pattern is in the skin underneath, so a shaved tiger is still striped"; "much of what we know about remaining numbers comes from exactly that"
correctedFact: Like a human fingerprint, no two tigers have exactly the same stripes. Researchers studying wild tigers use those patterns to tell individual animals apart, and camera trap studies are one of the tools scientists use to estimate how many tigers are left in places such as the mangrove forests of Bangladesh.
note: The skin pigmentation claim, which is the title, is on neither the Smithsonian nor the San Diego Zoo tiger page. Stripe identification and camera trap population work are supported.

quote: In most cases, the external shape is defined by a bony horn core, and the surface of the horn is only a thin sheath of hardened keratins (the same materials in fingernails and hair). Rhinoceros are unique in having large horns that are composed entirely of tiny keratin tubes embedded in a keratinous matrix, without any bony core. ... The tissue of rhinoceros horn itself, with its tubules-within-matrix architecture, is very similar to a number of other hardened skin appendages, including the hooves of horses and cattle, whale baleen, and the tips of bird beaks
unsupported: "structurally closer to an enormous callus" (the page compares horn tissue to hooves, baleen and bird beak tips, not a callus)
correctedFact: A rhino horn has no bony core at all. It is built entirely of tiny keratin tubes set in a keratin matrix, the same family of materials as fingernails and hair. Most horns, like a cow's, are a bony core under a thin keratin sheath. Rhino horn tissue is closer to a horse's hoof.
note: Lay summary of Hieronymus, Witmer and Ridgely (2006), Journal of Morphology 267(10).

pageTitle: UCT-led study finds dehorning rhinos drastically reduces poaching in key African stronghold
quote: “Dehorning rhinos to reduce incentives for poaching (2 284 rhinos were dehorned across eight reserves) was found to achieve a 78% reduction in poaching using just 1.2% of the overall rhino protection budget,” ... Some poaching for horn stumps and regrowth continued
unsupported: "Because there is no bone in it"; "cut above the growth plate"; "repeated every couple of years"; "the horn is used for defense and in disputes"
correctedFact: A rhino horn grows back after it is cut, which is why dehorning is used against poaching. In South Africa's Greater Kruger region, dehorning 2,284 rhinos cut poaching by 78 percent. It is not a clean fix: poachers still killed some dehorned rhinos for their horn stumps and regrowth.
note: News release for Kuiper et al. (2025) in Science, doi 10.1126/science.ado7490. The page is served as a PDF. Regrowth is implied by poaching for regrowth rather than stated outright.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2014)
pageTitle: A syndrome of mutualism reinforces the lifestyle of a sloth
quote: A three-toed sloth will, however, descend its tree weekly to defecate, which is risky, energetically costly and, until now, inexplicable. ... Descending a tree is both risky and energetically costly for any sloth. Indeed, it is the leading cause of mortality for a sloth; more than one-half of all adult sloth mortalities we have documented were depredation events when sloths were at or near the ground
unsupported: "On the ground it cannot walk and drags itself by its front claws"; "roughly fifty times a year" (follows from weekly but is not stated); "half of sloth predation deaths" (the paper says more than half of all documented adult deaths were predation at or near the ground)
correctedFact: About once a week, a three-toed sloth climbs down to the base of its tree to defecate, then climbs back up. It is the riskiest thing it does: in one study, more than half of all documented adult sloth deaths were predator kills made while the sloth was at or near the ground.
note: The paper's figure is a share of all adult deaths, which is a stronger statement than the card's share of predation deaths.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2014)
pageTitle: A syndrome of mutualism reinforces the lifestyle of a sloth
quote: Individual hairs of three-toed sloths possess unique transverse cracks, which allow the hair shaft to become saturated with rainwater, and which algae then colonize and grow hydroponically ... When a sloth descends a tree and defecates, gravid female moths leave the sloth and oviposit in the fresh excrement. ... Moths are portals for nutrients, increasing nitrogen levels in sloth fur, which fuels algal growth. Sloths consume these algae-gardens, presumably to augment their limited diet. ... this symbiotic alga is only known to inhabit the fur of sloths
unsupported: "grooves" (the paper says transverse cracks); "tints wild sloths green"; "It is contested but nothing better has replaced it"
correctedFact: Three-toed sloth hairs have cracks that soak up rainwater, and green algae known only from sloth fur grow in them. Moths live in the coat and lay their eggs in sloth dung during the weekly descent. One study proposed that the moths boost nitrogen in the fur, feeding the algae, which the sloths then eat.
note: Same paper as fact 255. It proposes the moth, algae and sloth mutualism; it does not discuss how contested the idea is.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: They have the largest ears relative to their body size of any member of the canid family, which they use to dispel heat and track down prey underneath the sand. ... They usually weigh between 2 and 3 pounds (0.9 to 1.4 kilograms). Perhaps their most notable characteristic is their ears, which can grow to between 4 to 6 inches (10.2 to 15.2 centimeters) in length. ... fennec foxes use their abnormally large ears to listen for prey underneath the sand, and once located will dig with all four feet to expose their meal.
unsupported: "of any carnivore" (the page says any member of the canid family); "a dense network of shallow blood vessels"; "without panting away water it cannot spare" (the same page says extreme panting helps fennecs regulate temperature, up to 690 breaths a minute)
correctedFact: A fennec's ears can grow to about 15 centimeters on an animal weighing roughly a kilogram, the largest ears for its body size of any member of the dog family. They are not only for listening. The fox uses them to shed heat, which matters for a small hunter living in the Sahara.
extraPoints: Fennecs hunt by ear, locating insects and rodents under the sand and digging straight down to them.
note: The panting line conflicts with the source, which lists extreme panting as one of the fennec's cooling methods.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Fennec foxes are also capable of going for long periods without consuming water; they are able to hydrate through the food they consume. ... They will also consume roots, fruits and leaves, which help them to hydrate. ... fennec foxes will hide out in burrows during daylight to avoid the hottest portion of the day.
unsupported: "go its whole life without drinking free water" (the page says long periods); "its kidneys concentrate urine"; "the air down in the den stays cooler and far more humid"; "in most of its range there is nothing to drink"
correctedFact: A fennec can go for long periods without drinking at all. It gets its water from food: the insects, rodents and lizards it hunts, plus roots, fruits and leaves that help keep it hydrated. It also spends the hottest part of the day underground, in burrows it digs itself.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Heavily furred paws provide traction when running in the sand while also offering protection from the extreme heat of the terrain. ... They create the burrows themselves, often digging out a series of tunnels that can reach up to 32 feet (10 meters) in length. It is not uncommon for these dens to have multiple entrances and exits to provide a safe escape
unsupported: "spreads the animal's weight so it can move across a loose surface without sinking" (the page says traction); "put itself out of sight underground in a few seconds"
correctedFact: The undersides of a fennec's feet are covered in thick fur, right over the pads. On desert sand that fur does two jobs: it protects the feet from the extreme heat of the ground, and it gives the fox traction when it runs across a loose surface.
extraPoints: Fennecs dig their own dens, tunnel systems up to 10 meters long with several entrances and exits.

pageTitle: What is the biggest snake in the world?
quote: Green anacondas, Eunectes murinus, are famously giant snakes. But they’ve also been subject to exaggerated length measurements in the past, with snakes of over 24 metres allegedly sighted. In reality, the green anaconda rarely exceeds 6.25 metres, making it significantly shorter than the biggest pythons. ... Green anacondas are the heaviest snakes in the world. The heaviest anaconda ever recorded was 227 kilograms. This massive snake was 8.43 metres long, with a girth of 1.11 metres. While the reticulated python is a longer snake, it’s also slender. Anacondas are bulky. It’s estimated that a 5.2-metre-long anaconda would weigh about the same as a 7.3-metre-long reticulated python.
unsupported: "Claims above nine meters have circulated for over a century without one being confirmed" (the page cites alleged sightings over 24 meters and a record 8.43 meter animal, with no time span)
correctedFact: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake alive, but not the longest. Reticulated pythons grow longer and slimmer: a 5.2 meter anaconda weighs about as much as a 7.3 meter python. The heaviest anaconda on record weighed 227 kilograms, and old claims of anacondas over 24 meters were exaggerations.
note: The python length claim holds: the page gives a 7.67 meter captive record and a 10 meter wild record from 1912. Smithsonian's anaconda page says adults can reach 9 meters, so the nine meter line may draw pushback.

pageTitle: Snake constriction rapidly induces circulatory arrest in rats
quote: The results demonstrate that within 6 s of being constricted, peripheral arterial blood pressure (PBP) at the femoral artery dropped to 1/2 of baseline values while central venous pressure (CVP) increased 6-fold from baseline during the same time. ... These results are the first to document the physiological response of prey to constriction and support the hypothesis that snake constriction induces rapid prey death due to circulatory arrest.
unsupported: "The snake tightens as its prey breathes out, so each exhalation gives away a little more room and never gets it back"; "far faster than suffocation would" (the abstract makes no comparison); the study used boas, not anacondas
correctedFact: Constriction kills mainly by stopping blood flow. When boas constricted rats in a 2015 study, the rats' arterial blood pressure halved within six seconds, and by the end nearly all showed failing heart rhythms. The researchers concluded that constriction causes rapid death through circulatory arrest.
note: Abstract only (PubMed); full text not fetched. Smithsonian's anaconda page still says anacondas suffocate their prey, so the site's own sources disagree.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Females are considerably larger than males. ... Green anacondas only mate every other year, likely due to the large amount of energy loss. Females give live birth in the water after sheltering through the rest of the dry season and can give birth to 20-40 young. The size of the litter is generally associated with the size of the female. The largest litter on record was 82 young.
unsupported: "each already around half a meter long and able to swim and hunt immediately"; "There is no parental care after that"; "a big female can be several times the weight of any male" (the page says considerably larger)
correctedFact: Green anacondas do not lay eggs. Females give birth to live young in the water, usually 20 to 40 at a time, and litter size tracks the size of the mother. The largest litter on record was 82 babies. Breeding is costly enough that females mate only every other year.
extraPoints: Female anacondas are far larger than males, unusual among snakes.

pageTitle: The Blue Dyeing Poison-Dart Frog, Dendrobates tinctorius (Dendrobates azureus, Hoogmoed 1969): extant in Suriname based on a rapid survey
quote: The blue color morph of Dendrobates tinctorius, originally described as D. azureus, has only been reported from a few forest islands surrounded by the Sipaliwini savanna in Suriname, South America. ... The Blue Dyeing Poison-dart Frog was described a half-century ago as Dendrobates azureus (Hoogmoed, 1969) and subsequently synonymized with D. tinctorius (Wollenberg et al. 2006). The inclusion of this species as a color morph of D. tinctorius was also confirmed by Noonan and Gaucher (2006).
unsupported: "one of the most photographed frogs on Earth"
correctedFact: The blue poison dart frog is not its own species. First described in 1969 as Dendrobates azureus, it was later folded into Dendrobates tinctorius as a color morph. It lives only on a few forest islands surrounded by the Sipaliwini savanna in southern Suriname, cut off from other populations.
note: Everything but the photography flourish is supported. The paper notes Ouboter and Jairam (2012) treat it as a subspecies, so 'local form' is the right framing.

pageTitle: Oribatid mites as a major dietary source for alkaloids in poison frogs
quote: Alkaloids in the skin glands of poison frogs serve as a chemical defense against predation, and almost all of these alkaloids appear to be sequestered from dietary arthropods. Certain alkaloid-containing ants have been considered the primary dietary source, but dietary sources for the majority of alkaloids remain unknown. ... Our findings suggest instead that mites exceed ants in importance as dietary sources of alkaloids in poison frogs.
unsupported: "Take that diet away and the toxicity goes with it"; "Captive-bred frogs raised on fruit flies and springtails are effectively non-toxic, which is why keeping one is possible at all and why a wild-caught animal is a completely different proposition"
correctedFact: Poison frogs do not make their own toxins. The alkaloids stored in their skin glands come almost entirely from what they eat. Ants were long thought to be the main source, but a 2007 study found about 80 alkaloids in tiny oribatid mites and concluded mites matter even more.
note: The captive claim, which is the card's title, is not in this paper. The study frog is Oophaga pumilio; the dietary point is made for poison frogs in general. Cached copy is the abstract; the Discussion quote was read from the PMC page.

pageTitle: Molecular phylogenetics uncovers two new species in the genus Phyllobates (Anura, Dendrobatidae): the terrible frog gets two new sisters
quote: True poison dart frogs (Phyllobates, Dendrobatidae) were discovered by Chocó indigenous people in western Colombia and used to poison blowgun darts by rubbing them on the frogs’ backs ... Only the Colombian species (P. terribilis, P. aurotaenia, and P. bicolor) were reportedly used to poison darts (Silverstone 1976; Myers et al. 1978).
unsupported: "Around 170 species get called poison dart frogs"; "in a small area"; "the coating stayed effective for months"
correctedFact: Of all the frogs called poison dart frogs, only three were ever reported to tip darts: Phyllobates terribilis, P. aurotaenia and P. bicolor, all from western Colombia. Indigenous Chocó hunters poisoned blowgun darts by rubbing them across a frog's back. Every other species, the blue poison dart frog included, borrowed the name.
note: This 2024 paper adds two new Phyllobates species, so the genus now has more than the three dart species, but only those three were used.

quote: The Victoria crowned pigeon, Goura victoria, and the Common crowned pigeon, Goura cristata, are the peacocks of the pigeon family. They are the largest surviving pigeons. The crowned pigeons, belonging to the family Gourinae, are large blue-gray birds with deep maroon below. ... possessing a large, fan-shaped crest of erect lacy feathers.
unsupported: "around 75 centimeters long and up to roughly 2.5 kilograms"; "a deep red eye"; "spends nearly all of its time walking the forest floor"; "northern" New Guinea (the page says New Guinea); "flies up mainly to roost or to get away from something"
correctedFact: The crowned pigeons are the largest pigeons alive, and the Victoria crowned pigeon is one of them: a big blue-gray bird with deep maroon underparts and a fan-shaped crest of upright, lacy feathers. Hunted for its crest and its meat, it has largely vanished near people but persists in the wilder forests of New Guinea.
note: Smithsonian and San Diego Zoo pages for this species return 404. The page credits both crowned pigeon species with largest status, not the Victoria alone.

quote: The most noticeable difference between these two pigeons is that the Victoria crowned pigeon’s crest is tipped in white while the Common crowned pigeon’s is not. ... possessing a large, fan-shaped crest of erect lacy feathers. The crest is so large and beautiful that these birds have been hunted as much as the birds of paradise.
unsupported: "Each feather in it has a bare shaft for most of its length and opens into a small triangular tip of white barbs at the end"; "Two other crowned pigeon species" (the page compares it with one, the common crowned pigeon)
correctedFact: The Victoria crowned pigeon wears a large, fan-shaped crest of upright, lacy feathers with white tips. That white edging is the quickest way to tell it from its close relative, the common crowned pigeon, whose crest has none. The crest is striking enough that these birds have been hunted for it.

quote: There is usually only one egg laid; it is elliptical in shape and white, with a faint bluish tinge. Male and female share incubating duties for about 30 days ... Pigeon or crop milk is a secretion of the adult crop which forms the complete diet of nestlings for the first few days of life. Crop milk is produced by both sexes.
unsupported: "protein and fat rich"; "It is not milk in any mammalian sense and contains no lactose" (the page says pigeon milk has a chemical composition similar to mammal milk); "the male through the day and the female overnight"
correctedFact: Pigeons feed their chicks on crop milk, a secretion of the adult's crop, and both the male and the female make it. A crowned pigeon chick lives on nothing else for its first few days. Pairs usually raise a single chick, and both parents share about 30 days of incubation.
note: The page's line that crop milk is chemically similar to mammal milk sits awkwardly with the card's 'not milk in any mammalian sense'.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: They have the second largest egg per body weight of any bird. ... The female lays a single extremely large egg — an average of 15 percent of her body weight. Producing such a large (about 1 pound) and energy-rich (over 60 percent yolk) eggs depletes the female's energy reserves. ... The kiwi's long, curved, pale gray-brown bill is unique in the bird world in having the nostrils located near the tip. They smell their prey rather than see it.
unsupported: "up to a fifth of the mother's body weight" (the page says an average of 15 percent); "the largest egg to body ratio of any bird alive" (the page says second largest); "the ostrich, whose egg is only about 2 percent of her weight"
correctedFact: A female kiwi lays a single, enormous egg averaging 15 percent of her body weight, about a pound of food that is over 60 percent yolk. Making it drains her reserves. Relative to body weight, it is the second largest egg of any bird alive.
extraPoints: Kiwis are the only birds with nostrils near the tip of the bill, and they find food by smell.
note: The source directly contradicts 'largest of any bird alive'; it does not name the bird in first place.

pageTitle: Facts About the Greyhound That You May Not Know
quote: The Greyhound is a sighthound, which means they chase game based on their sight instead of by scent. ... In addition to being the fastest dog breed, Greyhounds are one of the fastest animals, period. In fact, Greyhounds have been clocked at more than 35 miles per hour, with the world record sitting at 41.83 miles per hour.
unsupported: "up to 45 miles per hour" (the AKC gives a world record of 41.83 mph)
correctedFact: Greyhounds are the fastest dog breed, clocked at more than 35 miles per hour, with a world record of 41.83. They are sighthounds, which means they chase game by eyesight rather than by scent. They are known for agility, endurance and extraordinary speed.
note: The AKC breed page itself has no speed figure. The 45 mph number circulates on pet sites; the AKC uses 35 to 45 mph only for dogs in general on its Fast CAT page.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Orangutans are the largest arboreal mammals and are very well adapted to life in the trees, with arms much longer than their legs. They have grasping hands and feet with long curved fingers and toes. ... They are highly arboreal and live in all levels of the forest, from floor to canopy.
unsupported: "arm span can stretch up to 7 feet"; "more than 95 percent of their time up in the canopy"; "Shoulder and hip joints that rotate more freely than a human's"; "largest tree-dwelling animals on Earth" (the page says mammals)
correctedFact: Orangutans are the largest tree-dwelling mammals, with arms much longer than their legs and grasping hands and feet with long, curved fingers and toes. They can swing hand over hand, but usually move cautiously by climbing and walking along branches, spreading their weight. On the ground they are slow and awkward.

quote: Although shark-like in appearance, sawfishes are actually rays, as their gills and mouths are found on the undersides of their bodies. ... The rostrum also contains an electro-sensory system, which can sense the weak amount of electricity produced by other animals. This system helps sawfish identify when prey is nearby.
unsupported: "packed with thousands of electroreceptor pores"; "find prey buried in sand or mud without ever seeing it"
correctedFact: Despite their shark-like shape, sawfish are rays, with their gills and mouths on the underside of the body. Their long, toothed snout, the rostrum, carries an electrosensory system that picks up the faint electricity other animals give off, telling a sawfish when prey is nearby.

pageTitle: One size does not fit all: Variation in anatomical traits associated with emersion behavior in mudskippers (Gobiidae: Oxudercinae)
quote: The skin is important in mudskippers as cutaneous respiration is a primary respiration method for some species when out of water, although gills are also used (Tamura et al., 1976) as well as bucco-opercular cavity (Ishimatsu, 2017). ... These traits include an increase in capillary density in the skin allowing for more absorption, as well as a decrease in the distance between those capillaries and the surface of the skin
unsupported: "for hours"; "up to 60 percent of the oxygen they need on land"; "prop themselves up on their front fins like little arms to hop across mudflats and even climb mangrove roots"; "as long as their skin stays wet"
correctedFact: Mudskippers are fish that spend long stretches out of water, and for some species the skin is a main way to breathe air. Dense capillaries close to the skin's surface help it absorb oxygen, and they also take in oxygen through their gills and the chamber of the mouth and gill covers.
extraPoints: Mudskippers move on land by propping themselves on their front fins, hopping across mud and climbing mangrove roots.
note: The paper also notes that species differ: some take up oxygen better in air, others rely more on water.

quote: Note that the upper molars are rotated 90 degrees inward, which is the identifying dentition characteristic of the family Mustelidae (weasel family). This is one of the structural features that has made the wolverine successful as a predator/scavenger, enabling it to crush bones and consume frozen tissue.
unsupported: "about 15 kilograms"; "take marrow that other scavengers walk away from"; "which is most of how a wolverine gets through a northern winter"
correctedFact: A wolverine's upper molars are turned 90 degrees inward, a dental hallmark of the whole weasel family. In the wolverine it is one of the features that makes a scavenging life work, helping it crush bones and eat frozen tissue from the carcasses it finds.
note: The rotation is shared by all mustelids, so the card should not imply it is unique to wolverines.

quote: The skull and teeth are robust and the musculature, especially of the head, neck and shoulders, is well developed. ... Typical weights for adult males are 12-18 kg and for adult females, 8-12 kg. ... The wolverine has been described as "the fiercest creature on earth" (Ferguson 1969), "vicious," a "dangerous killer," and "a fearless aggressive fighter" who "will drive bears away from their kills" (Winkley and Fallon 1974). ... Not a hunter, it depends on wolves and other predators to provide carrion, and contrary to legend, is at times killed by these carnivores.
unsupported: "driving wolves ... off a carcass" (the chapter says wolves sometimes kill wolverines); "repeated accounts" (bear driving is cited only as reputation); "thick hide"; "no apparent reverse gear"; "a larger animal often decides the meal is not worth the trouble"; "12 to 18 kilograms" applies to adult males only (females 8 to 12)
correctedFact: Adult male wolverines typically weigh 12 to 18 kilograms and females 8 to 12, yet the species has a reputation as a fearless fighter said to drive bears away from their kills. The reputation outruns the record: wolverines rely on wolves and other predators for carrion, and are sometimes killed by them.
note: The source treats the bear story as legend and stresses that wolverines are killed by wolves; the card's title claim needs softening.
